ask: Why is it on the path?
cards: The prophet whose hymns, the Gathas, stand at the origin of Zoroastrianism; his dates are disputed by a thousand years, most scholars favouring the late second millennium BCE.
Faith of the Achaemenid kings and state religion of the Parthians and Sasanians, whose ideas of judgement, heaven and hell may have influenced Judaism, Christianity and Islam.
The Wise Lord, first notably invoked in the Behistun Inscription of Darius the Great and later named in royal inscriptions in a triad with Mithra and Anahita.
An Indo-Iranian god of covenant, truth and light, venerated in the Avesta and shown on Kushan coins, distinct from, though related to, the Mithras of Rome.
A Roman mystery cult of soldiers and merchants who met in cave-like temples; Cumont saw it as the Roman form of Persian religion, a model scholars have generally rejected since the 1970s.
A centralised Zoroastrian monarchy that ruled Iran and Mesopotamia from 224 to 651 and was Rome’s great rival for four centuries, until the Arab conquests ended it.
Founded by the prophet Mani in Sasanian Mesopotamia about 240, it taught a struggle of light and darkness and spread from Roman North Africa to China.
Descendants of Zoroastrians who left Iran after the Arab conquest, this community of western India preserved the old state faith of the Sasanian Empire.
Given its lasting form by Sheikh Adi at Lalish, the faith of the Peacock Angel remembers 74 campaigns of destruction, among them the genocide at Sinjar in 2014.
Heralded by the Báb in Shiraz in 1844 and founded by Bahá’u’lláh, it teaches the oneness of God, of religion and of humanity, and has been persecuted in Iran from its beginnings.
